label: Fuel
summary: Petrol, diesel, kerosene and propane burn easily and their vapour can explode. Petrol vapour and propane are heavier than air: they flow along floors and pool in pits, basements and low spots, where a pilot light, switch or spark sets them off.
signs: Smell of petrol, diesel or gas
Rainbow sheen on puddles, or stained ground
Cans, drums, cylinders and vehicles; tanks under petrol station forecourts
Hissing, or frost on a gas cylinder valve or hose
Bubbles when soapy water is brushed on a fitting
do: Store fuel outside or in a ventilated shed, away from where people sleep
Use proper fuel cans with tight caps
Put cans on the ground while filling so static can drain away
Wipe up spills and let the vapour clear before starting anything
Keep a fire extinguisher, sand or a fire blanket close to fuel
Smell gas in a building: don't work switches, phones or flames; shut the cylinder or meter valve if you can do it safely, open doors and windows, and get out
dont: Don't siphon by mouth: fuel in the lungs causes a severe pneumonia
Don't smoke or make sparks near fuel or open cans
Don't use petrol to clean parts or to start a fire
Don't fill cans standing in a vehicle or on a plastic truck bed liner
Don't store propane cylinders indoors or in basements
Don't throw water on burning fuel: it spreads the fire
Never put petrol in a kerosene (paraffin) or diesel heater, lamp or stove: it flares up and can explode
ppe: Nitrile gloves; petrol soaks through skin
Safety glasses when pouring or draining
Cotton or wool clothes; synthetics melt onto skin in a fire
firstAid: Fuel on skin: wash with soap and water; take off soaked clothing and keep it away from flames
Fuel in an eye: rinse with clean water for at least 15 minutes
Swallowed fuel: don't make them vomit; get medical help, especially if they cough or are short of breath
Breathed vapour: get to fresh air; confusion or collapse needs medical care
Burns: cool under cool running water for 20 minutes and cover loosely; large or deep burns need medical care
Clothing on fire: stop, drop to the ground and roll, or smother the flames with a coat or blanket; then cool the burns
